derivations.claim: The orthogonality in [F1] gives $\psi=\sum_\lambda P_\lambda\psi$ and $\|\psi\|^2=\sum_\lambda\|P_\lambda\psi\|^2=1$. Thus the weights in [F2] are nonnegative and sum to one. By [F5]–[F6], $\langle\psi|g(H)|\psi\rangle=\sum_\lambda g(\lambda)\langle\psi|P_\lambda|\psi\rangle=\sum_\lambda\mu_\psi(\{\lambda\})g(\lambda)$.

By linearity, the QPE unitary sends the initial phase state and $\psi$ to $\sum_\lambda\sum_y a_y(\lambda)|y\rangle\otimes P_\lambda\psi$, using [F3] on each eigenspace. Projecting the phase register onto $|y\rangle$ gives the system vector $v_y=\sum_\lambda a_y(\lambda)P_\lambda\psi$. Since the summands for distinct $\lambda$ are orthogonal by [F1], [F4] yields $\Pr(Y=y)=\|v_y\|^2=\sum_\lambda |a_y(\lambda)|^2\|P_\lambda\psi\|^2=\sum_\lambda\mu_\psi(\{\lambda\})P_{\theta(\lambda)}(y)$. Summing these probabilities over the finite output set gives one, as each eigenphase kernel is a measurement law.

When $\Pr(Y=y)>0$, [F4] normalizes the projected branch to $v_y/\|v_y\|$, which is the displayed formula. Its coefficients $a_y(\lambda)$ need not vanish outside one eigenvalue, so no exact eigenspace-collapse claim follows; the formula itself gives the precise conditional state.

derivations.claim: On a Hermitian input $A$, each active parity singular-value transform in [F4] equals ordinary polynomial functional calculus. Indeed, for an eigenvector with eigenvalue $x>0$, choose its left and right singular vectors equal, so its transform coefficient is $p_j(x)$. For $x<0$, choose singular value $|x|$ and left vector the negative of the right vector; the coefficient is $-p_j(|x|)=p_j(x)$ when $p_j$ is odd, while for even parity it is $p_j(|x|)=p_j(x)$. At $x=0$, an odd polynomial vanishes and the even transform assigns $p_j(0)$ on the kernel. The spectral resolution [F7] and basis-independence in [F4] make these equalities independent of choices within degenerate eigenspaces. Also [F1] gives $|f(\lambda)|\le\sum_{j\in J}\gamma_j=B$ on $\sigma(H)$; apply [F2] to the zero polynomial and $f$ to obtain $\|f(H)\|\le B$.

By [F2], $\|p_j(A)-g_j(H)/\gamma_j\|\le\tau_j$, since $A=H/\alpha$ and the scalar bound holds on its spectrum. By [F3]–[F4], replacing the exact signal block $A$ by $\widetilde A$ changes the ideal transform $p_j^{\mathrm{SV}}$ by at most $4d_j\sqrt{\varepsilon_{BE}}$; step 1.1 identifies the transform at $A$ with $p_j(A)$. The implemented component adds at most $\kappa_j$ by its definition, including numerical phase and signal implementation errors. For any unit vector $v$, the vector triangle inequality in [F9] bounds the action of the total difference by the sum of these three operator bounds; taking the supremum over unit $v$ gives $\|Y_j-g_j(H)/\gamma_j\|\le\tau_j+4d_j\sqrt{\varepsilon_{BE}}+\kappa_j$, where $Y_j$ is its actual top-left block.

The exact LCU block for these $Y_j$ is $B^{-1}\sum_{j\in J}c_j\gamma_jY_j$ by [F5]; its actual circuit differs from that block by at most $\kappa_{LCU}$. The decomposition in [F1] gives $f(H)=\sum_{j\in J}c_jg_j(H)$ on the spectrum. For each unit vector $v$, apply the vector triangle inequality [F9] to the weighted sum of component errors from step 2.1 and the LCU implementation error; taking the supremum over $v$ gives the displayed operator-norm bound after multiplying each component bound by $\gamma_j/B$.

The exact signal-call count for component $j\in J$ is $d_j$ by [F8]; a SELECT branch invokes its designated component sequence, so no path uses more than $\max_{j\in J}d_j$ base signal calls in that SELECT. The remaining resource coordinates are the declared preparation, inverse, control, coefficient, phase, reflection, compilation, and output costs in [F1], [F6], and [F8]; neither a degree count nor an exact phase list supplies those costs automatically.

derivations.claim: For an exact eigenvector of eigenvalue $\lambda\in[-1,1]$, [F9] identifies the encoded phase as $\theta=\lambda/(2\pi)$ modulo one, with $|\theta|\le1/(2\pi)$. Set $\eta=\epsilon/(2\pi)$; then $Q\eta=Q\epsilon/(2\pi)\ge3$, so $K=\lfloor Q\eta\rfloor\ge3$. By [F1], except with probability at most $1/(2(K-1))\le1/4$, the circular phase error is less than $\eta$. On this success event the phase estimate has a representative $\widehat\theta=\theta+e$ with $|e|<\eta\le1/(2\pi)$; since $|\widehat\theta|<1/\pi<1/2$ by [F7], it is exactly the principal representative, so the decoded eigenvalue error is $2\pi|e|<\epsilon$. Thus each exact trial succeeds with probability at least $3/4$.

With controlled-$U$ access, the QPE phase register uses powers $U^{2^j}$ for $j=0,\ldots,m-1$, whose repeated-call implementation uses $\sum_j2^j=Q-1$ calls per trial. There are $r$ trials; each begins with a fresh charged state preparation and has one projective readout and one decoder. Exact supplied powers replace this count by their declared per-trial costs. No uncontrolled resource coordinate is inferred.

The rational schedule search in [F2] terminates. Since $\epsilon>0$ and $\pi_+,L_+$ are finite rationals, [F8] gives an integer $N\ge1$ with $N>6\pi_+/\epsilon$ and $N>8L_+$. The bound $2^n\ge n+1$ follows by induction: it is equality at $n=0$, and $2^{n+1}\ge2(n+1)\ge n+2$ whenever it holds at $n$. Thus $2^N\epsilon\ge(N+1)\epsilon>6\pi_+$ and the dyadic doubling search stops by exponent $N$. The odd integer $2N+1$ exceeds $8L_+$, so the increasing odd search also stops by then. Each least schedule value is therefore found by a finite search, with rational comparisons.

Let $X_i$ be the indicator of success on trial $i$ and $S=\sum_{i=1}^rX_i$. Exact independent fresh preparations make the $X_i$ independent, with $p_i=\Pr(X_i=1)\ge3/4$ by step 1.1. For $t=\ln3>0$, on $S\le r/2$ we have $e^{-tS}\ge e^{-tr/2}$, so summing the nonnegative finite expectation over this event gives $\Pr(S\le r/2)\le e^{tr/2}\mathbb E(e^{-tS})=e^{tr/2}\prod_i(1-p_i+p_ie^{-t})\le(\sqrt3/2)^r$. Each factor decreases in $p_i$ and at $p_i=3/4$ the product factor is $\sqrt3(1/4+1/4)=\sqrt3/2$. Since $2/\sqrt3>8/7$ (both sides are positive and $4/3>64/49$ because $196>192$) and [F5] gives $\ln(8/7)=\int_1^{8/7}dt/t\ge1/8$, we have $(\sqrt3/2)^r\le e^{-r/8}$. The schedule gives $r/8\ge L_+\ge\ln(1/\delta)$, so [F6] and monotonicity of the exponential yield $e^{-r/8}\le e^{-\ln(1/\delta)}=\delta$. An odd median is inaccurate only if at least half the trials are inaccurate, which is contained in $\{S\le r/2\}$; this proves the exact claim.

For one approximate trial, write the exact and implemented normalized vectors as $v,w$. For each phase-register projector $P_y$, expand $\langle v,P_yv\rangle-\langle w,P_yw\rangle=\langle v-w,P_yv\rangle+\langle w,P_y(v-w)\rangle$. By [F4] and orthogonality, Cauchy–Schwarz bounds each sum over $y$ of the absolute values of these two terms by $\|v-w\|$; hence the $\ell^1$ distance of the outcome laws is at most $2\xi$ and their total variation distance (one half of that distance) is at most $\xi$. Telescoping the $r$ product laws one factor at a time gives total variation at most $r\xi$, since every unchanged factor is a probability law of mass one. Therefore any median-success event has probability at least its exact probability minus $r\xi$, yielding $1-\delta-r\xi$.

The eigenstate promise cannot be dropped from the generic phase-access procedure. Consider the access instance $U=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)$ with encoded eigenvalue labels $0$ and $1/2$ assigned to phases $0$ and $1/2$, and input $\psi=(|0\rangle+|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$. Choose any $0<\epsilon<1/4$ and a dyadic $Q$ satisfying $Q\epsilon\ge6\pi$; then $Q$ is even. Both phases lie exactly on the QPE grid, so [F1] gives output $0$ or $1/2$ with probability $1/2$ each. Fresh repetitions are independent; pairing each length-$r$ sequence with the sequence obtained by swapping every $0$ and $1/2$ shows the median is each encoded eigenvalue with probability exactly $1/2$. The two $\epsilon$-neighborhoods are disjoint, so neither fixed label has success probability above $1/2$. This counterexample uses the generic injective phase-encoding interface [F3], and shows why this theorem states the Hamiltonian guarantee for eigenstate input only.

**Inputs.** A nonzero finite-dimensional Hermitian matrix $H$, a scale $\alpha>0$ with $\|H\|\le\alpha$, a supplied block encoding of $H/\alpha$, a function $f$ on $\sigma(H)$, and a caller-supplied extension $\bar f:[-\alpha,\alpha]\to\mathbb C$ agreeing with $f$ on the spectrum. Let $J$ be a nonempty subset of $\{0,1,2,3\}$. For each $j\notin J$, supply an exact certificate that $g_j$ is identically zero on $[-\alpha,\alpha]$. For each $j\in J$, supply a positive scale $\gamma_j$ satisfying $|g_j(t)|\le\gamma_j$ on that interval, a tolerance $\tau_j\ge0$, and a real polynomial $p_j$ of declared parity and degree $d_j$ with $|p_j(x)|\le1$ on $[-1,1]$ and
$$\left|p_j(x)-\frac{g_j(\alpha x)}{\gamma_j}\right|\le\tau_j\qquad(-1\le x\le1),$$
where
$$g_0(t)=\frac{\Re\bar f(t)+\Re\bar f(-t)}2,\quad g_1(t)=\frac{\Re\bar f(t)-\Re\bar f(-t)}2,$$
$$g_2(t)=\frac{\Im\bar f(t)+\Im\bar f(-t)}2,\quad g_3(t)=\frac{\Im\bar f(t)-\Im\bar f(-t)}2.$$
Thus $g_0,g_2$ are even, $g_1,g_3$ are odd, and $\bar f=g_0+g_1+i g_2+i g_3$. The zero certificates and scale bounds give $|\bar f(t)|\le B:=\sum_{j\in J}\gamma_j$; the construction makes no optimal-normalization claim. For an identically zero target one may take $J=\{0\}$, $\gamma_0=1$, and $p_0=0$.

If the block encoding, phase operations, and LCU operations are exact, all $\kappa$ terms vanish. The scale $B$ is the supplied sum of component scales, not an asserted optimal normalization.

derivations.claim: Let $S=\sqrt{I-H^2}=\operatorname{diag}(\sqrt3/2,2\sqrt2/3)$ and set $U=\begin{pmatrix}H&S\\S&-H\end{pmatrix}$. Since $S=S^*$, $H=H^*$, and $HS=SH$, $U^*=U$ and $U^2=\begin{pmatrix}H^2+S^2&HS-SH\\SH-HS&S^2+H^2\end{pmatrix}=I$. Thus $U$ is unitary and its top-left block is $H$, proving the exact dilation assertion by [F1].

The real part of $e^{-ix}$ is even and the imaginary part is $-\sin x$, which is odd, by [F3]. For phase list $(0)$ the degree-zero signal sequence has upper-left entry $1$. For $(\pi/2,\pi/2)$, the upper-left entry of $Z(\pi/2)W_R(x)Z(\pi/2)$ is $x e^{i\pi}=-x$, by the sequence definition [F2]. Using the exact dilation from step 1.1, the polynomials have matching parity and satisfy $|p_R(x)|=1$, $|p_I(x)|\le1$ on $[-1,1]$. The coefficient weights are both one, so the LCU scale is $B=2$; by [F2] its normalized weighted sum is $(I+i(-H))/2=(I-iH)/2$, with the stated normalization.

For $|x|\le1$, the alternating cosine series has decreasing terms after its constant term, so [F4] gives $|1-\cos x|\le x^2/2$; its sine series analogously gives $|x-\sin x|\le|x|^3/6$. On the two eigenvalues these imply component errors $\tau_0\le1/8$ and $\tau_3\le1/48$. With $\varepsilon_{BE}=0$, exact phases and exact LCU, the error formula in [F2] gives normalized block error at most $(1/8+1/48)/2=7/96$. Equivalently, $|(1-ix)/2-e^{-ix}/2|\le(|1-\cos x|+|x-\sin x|)/2\le(x^2/2+|x|^3/6)/2$, which is $7/96$ at $x=-1/2$ and $5/162$ at $x=1/3$. The scalar error is at most $7/96$ on $\sigma(H)$; applying the polynomial matrix-function transfer theorem [F2] to $p(x)=(1-ix)/2$ and $f(x)=e^{-ix}/2$ gives the same operator-norm bound.

Let $H$ be a Hermitian endomorphism of a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space, with distinct eigenvalues $\lambda$ and orthogonal spectral projections $P_\lambda$. Let $\psi$ be a unit vector representing a pure state. Its **state-dependent spectral distribution** is the finite measure on $\sigma(H)$ defined by
$$\mu_\psi(\{\lambda\})=\|P_\lambda\psi\|^2=\langle\psi|P_\lambda|\psi\rangle.$$
The support is restricted to eigenvalues with nonzero weight; degeneracies are represented by one atom per distinct eigenvalue, not one atom per chosen eigenvector. The formula is the definition; its nonnegativity, total mass one, and functional-calculus moment identity are established in [[thm-qa-28-spectral-law-measurement]].

Let $H$ be Hermitian with distinct eigenvalues $\lambda$, spectral projections $P_\lambda$, and normalized input $\psi$. Run the ideal phase-estimation sampler on $\psi$, with unitary $U$ whose eigenphase on $P_\lambda V$ is the declared $\theta(\lambda)$. Write $a_y(\lambda)$ for the phase-register amplitude at output $y$ when the input is in that eigenspace, so $|a_y(\lambda)|^2=P_{\theta(\lambda)}(y)$ as in [[lem-qa-phase-estimation-outcome-kernel]]. Then the output law is
$$\Pr(Y=y)=\sum_{\lambda\in\sigma(H)}\mu_\psi(\{\lambda\})P_{\theta(\lambda)}(y).$$
For every outcome with positive probability, the normalized conditional system vector is
$$\psi_y=\frac{\sum_\lambda a_y(\lambda)P_\lambda\psi}{\sqrt{\Pr(Y=y)}}.$$
Moreover, $\mu_\psi$ is a probability distribution and, for every $g:\sigma(H)\to\mathbb C$,
$$\langle\psi|g(H)|\psi\rangle=\sum_\lambda\mu_\psi(\{\lambda\})g(\lambda).$$
The conditional system is generally a coherent sum across eigenspaces, not an exact eigenspace projection.

If $Q\theta$ is an integer $t$, then $P_\theta(t)=1$ and all other labels have probability $0$.

derivations.claim: The two diagonal entries are distinct, so their spectral projections are $|0\rangle\langle0|$ and $|1\rangle\langle1|$. Their action on $\psi$ gives squared norms $3/5$ and $2/5$, respectively; the squares sum to one. By [F1], these are exactly the masses and the measured phase law is $\frac35P_{-1/(4\pi)}+\frac25P_{1/(6\pi)}$.

We certify $\pi<4$. The sine Taylor partial sum through $-4^7/7!$ is $S_3=4-4^3/3!+4^5/5!-4^7/7!=-6976/5040=-502272/362880$. Starting with $4^9/9!$, the absolute Taylor terms decrease because the next-to-current ratio is $16/((n+1)(n+2))<1$ for odd $n\ge7$; [F4] therefore bounds the alternating remainder by $4^9/9!=262144/362880$. Hence $\sin4\le-240128/362880<0$. By [F3], sine is positive on $(0,2]$, while continuity and the negative value at $4$ give a zero in $(2,4)$ by the intermediate value theorem. Its first positive zero is $\pi$, so $\pi<4$.

For either phase, put $\eta=\epsilon/(2\pi)=1/(8\pi)$. Then $Q\eta=16/\pi>4$ by $\pi<4$, so $K=\lfloor Q\eta\rfloor\ge4$; [F2] bounds the circular tail by at most $1/6<1/4$. On this success event the phase estimate has a lift within $\eta$ of $\theta=\lambda/(2\pi)$; since $|\theta|\le1/(2\pi)$ and $\eta=1/(8\pi)$, the lift has magnitude at most $5/(8\pi)<1/2$ by $\pi>2$, so it is the principal representative and the decoded eigenvalue error is at most $\epsilon$. Thus each eigenstate has success at least $3/4$. By [F1], the total success probability is at least $(3/5)(3/4)+(2/5)(3/4)=3/4$. The eigenvalue gap is $1/3-(-1/2)=5/6>1/2=2\epsilon$, so the two intervals are disjoint.
The seven phase bits require the controlled powers with exponents $1,2,4,8,16,32,64$. Repeating controlled-$U$ for each power uses $1+2+4+8+16+32+64=127$ calls.
